pages.title: NEURODIVERSITY & DECOLONISING DESIGN.
pages.intro: We started with autism and interviews, and asked who gets to decide what “good” design means.

children.text:
AUTISM, MORE THAN ONE WAY OF EXPERIENCING THINGS
We started by learning about autism. Things like loud sounds, bright lights and being around lots of people can feel very different for different people. We also talked about stimming. Sometimes a repeated movement or action helps someone feel more comfortable, so we shouldn’t be too quick to judge what we see.

INTERVIEWS ARE NOT JUST A LIST OF QUESTIONS
The teacher showed us how to ask open questions and give people time to answer. I think this is important because we are trying to understand someone’s everyday life, not get them to say what we want to hear.

WHO GETS TO DECIDE WHAT GOOD DESIGN IS?
We also covered Decolonising Design. It made us look at how culture, language and power can affect what people think is normal or good. Something that works in one place might not work the same way somewhere else. We need to hear from the people who actually live there.

A WORD FOR MY FUTURE SELF
In one activity, we picked words about our future. I chose “stories”. I like listening to other people’s stories because I can always learn something new from a world that isn’t mine.

DIFFERENT PEOPLE, DIFFERENT EVERYDAY TASKS
At the end, we talked about disability, Universal Design and barriers in the environment. We even tried small tasks involving memory, attention and planning. They sounded simple, but they helped us look at everyday tasks from another angle.

pages.title: UNDERSTANDING DIFFERENT NEEDS.
pages.intro: Autism, sensory maps and a guest whose way of listening really surprised me.

sections.name: 01 / VISUAL IMPAIRMENT GUEST INTERVIEW — Photo Left, Notes Right

children.name: PHOTO / CLASS INTERVIEW — REPLACE IMAGE HERE

children.text: We met a guest with visual impairment who talked about using sound, touch and familiar clues in daily life. What surprised me was that he could follow audio at about twice the normal speed! I could barely keep up. We also asked about navigation tools and how helpful they really are.

For our group discussion, we looked at autism and travelling by MRT. Loud sounds, crowds and sudden changes can make the journey difficult for some people. But we also learned that not everyone with autism has the same sensory needs.

ABC stands for Antecedent, Behaviour and Consequence. The idea is to look at what happens before and after a behaviour, rather than deciding too quickly what it means. The teacher also introduced picture cards, co-regulation and visual schedules as ways to help with communication.

One example I remember from class was the sensory map at Changi Airport. It shows what visitors can expect in different areas, which can be useful for someone planning a trip. We also talked about clear signs and information when people go somewhere unfamiliar.

pages.title: CARE, COMMUNITY & DEAF ACCESSIBILITY.
pages.intro: From caregivers to Deaf communication, we looked at the people and services around everyday life.

children.text:
THE PEOPLE WHO TAKE CARE OF OTHERS
One topic this week was caregivers. Looking after a family member can take up so much time and energy, and the caregiver also needs support. When we talk about designing for someone with a disability, it is easy to forget the other people involved in their daily life.

COMMUNITY CARE
We looked at examples from Singapore and the Netherlands. Care doesn’t only happen inside a hospital or care centre. The neighbourhood, family and community services around a person can also make a big difference. The examples helped us see how many things need to work together.

COMMUNICATION WITHOUT SOUND
The lesson also covered Deaf and hard-of-hearing people. Think about a train announcement or an alarm: if the information is only spoken, not everyone can receive it. Captions, visual alerts and sign language are useful examples. We also learned that sign languages differ around the world.

UNDERSTANDING DIFFERENT LEVELS OF SUPPORT
We were introduced to intellectual disability and how some people may need more time, clear steps or pictures to understand information. We came back to Human-Centred Design too. We cannot decide what someone needs only from our own point of view; we need to understand how they actually do things.

pages.title: ACCESSIBILITY & SOCIAL SERVICES.
pages.intro: Ramps, lifts, signs and even the height of a counter — lots of small details to check.

children.text:
ACCESSIBILITY IS IN THE SMALL DETAILS
This class was much more about the actual size and position of things. For a wheelchair user, the space to turn, the height of a counter, where a screen is placed and how a door opens all matter. A building might have a ramp or lift and still be difficult to use.

WHAT SHOULD WE LOOK FOR ON SITE?
Our group started listing what we needed to check in the MRT station: the route, signs, corners, machines and whether everything is easy to reach. We also needed to arrange our ideas for a presentation and prepare to test them in the real space.

HOW DO SOCIAL SERVICES KEEP WORKING?
Another part of the lesson was about running social service organisations. Even a useful service needs enough money, people and space to continue. Families can have completely different situations, so there isn’t one perfect solution for everyone.

POEMS
We learned a research method called POEMS: People, Objects, Environments, Messages and Services. Instead of only taking photos of a space, it reminds us to look at what people are doing, what they use and how the whole service works. There are usually more details than we first notice.

pages.title: UNIVERSAL DESIGN & HUMAN-CENTRED SPACES.
pages.intro: Universal Design and Maggie’s Centres showed us different ways to make a space feel welcoming.

children.text:
DESIGN ISN’T ONLY FOR THE “AVERAGE” PERSON
We went through Universal Design and why a design should consider different people from the beginning. Not everyone moves, sees or uses a space in the same way. If we only design for one kind of user, other people have to keep finding ways around it.

ONE SPACE, DIFFERENT NEEDS
A step-free entrance might help a wheelchair user, but it also helps someone with a stroller or heavy luggage. Clear signs and doors that are easy to open can be useful to many people. It isn’t always necessary to give everyone a completely separate space.

MAGGIE’S CENTRES
I liked this example because it looks very different from what I normally imagine when I think of a healthcare space. Maggie’s Centres support people affected by cancer, but they have gardens, natural light, kitchens and places to sit together. It feels more like a home than a hospital. The space considers people’s feelings as well as their practical needs.

THE SEVEN PRINCIPLES
We also looked at the seven principles of Universal Design, such as flexible use, clear information, low physical effort and enough room to move. The teacher compared Universal Design and Inclusive Design and talked about cost too. A nice idea still has to work in real life.

pages.title: PRESENTATION PREPARATION — NO CLASS.
pages.intro: No regular class — we used the time to sort out our slides and presentation.

children.text:
NO NORMAL CLASS THIS WEEK
We didn’t have a usual lesson. The teacher gave us time to work on our group presentation, sort out the PPT and practise what we were going to say. Most of the week was spent putting our ideas together and getting ready to present.

pages.title: SMALL DETAILS, BIG DIFFERENCES.
pages.intro: A guest interview, a sign language lesson and some interesting details from everyday life.

sections.name: 01 / Deaf Guest Interview · Photo Left and Notes Right

children.name: INTERVIEW PHOTO / REPLACE IMAGE HERE → Fill

children.text: This week we met a Deaf man whose wife is also Deaf. They have two lovely daughters. He taught us some sign language and answered our questions about travelling. What caught my attention wasn’t only public transport, but also the little ways their family had adapted their home.

He shared a small detail from home: a bell near a room door that helps the family notice when someone comes in. It was such a simple idea, but I hadn’t really thought about designing a home like that before.

sections.name: 03 / WHY THE CLASSROOM WAS ARRANGED IN A CURVE

children.text: 03 / WHY THE CLASSROOM WAS ARRANGED IN A CURVE

When we learned sign language, the seats were arranged in a semicircle. That way, everyone could see each other’s faces. I noticed that communication wasn’t only about hand movements. Facial expressions can also show a lot of feelings.
The bell and the semicircle seating were the two details I remembered most from the guest session. They were small things in everyday life, but both had a clear reason behind them.

pages.title: DESIGN ETHNOGRAPHY & DI SOCIAL SERVICES.
pages.intro: A social service design case study, plus a look at how community services work behind the scenes.

children.text:
THE PATH TO… / A SOCIAL SERVICE DESIGN CASE STUDY

WHERE THE RESEARCH STARTED
We looked at The Path To… Designing Social Services in Singapore, a project by Veryday and DesignSingapore Council. Before making any designs, the team went out to understand people’s lives. They spoke to people with disabilities, caregivers and organisations. The presentation mentioned 24 interviews, more than five welfare organisations, over 120 hours of video and over 6,000 images. That is a lot of material to sort through!

MORE THAN JUST ONE PROBLEM
The research was organised into 12 areas, including family, self-image, culture, policies, housing, money, assistive technology and transport. I found it interesting that these issues were so connected. Even if someone has the right wheelchair, they may still have trouble leaving home because the transport is difficult or expensive.

INDEPENDENCE AND BEING TREATED DIFFERENTLY
Some of the people in the study worried about being a burden or being treated differently. Their difficulties weren’t only about the physical environment. Having fewer choices can also affect someone’s confidence and daily relationships.

WHAT ABOUT THE FAMILY?
The case study included caregivers too. Some parents and family members spent so much time caring for others that they barely had time for themselves. There were also worries about money and the future. It showed why the people around the main user should not be left out.

SERVICES, TECHNOLOGY AND EVERYDAY LIFE
We saw how staff, funding and training affect what social service organisations can provide. Assistive technology can help, but the price and learning process can also become a problem. Housing and transport came up as well. Some people didn’t have much personal space at home, while others struggled to get to work or activities. The transport problems felt very close to what we had been investigating in the MRT.

DI CLASS DISCUSSION / HOW SERVICES ACTUALLY RUN

DIGITAL SYSTEMS AND AI
Another class looked at digital systems. We heard about building AI tools that are reliable and safe, testing them properly and making sure staff know how to use them. A new system is not much help if the people using it haven’t been trained.

CHILDREN AND FAMILY SUPPORT
There were examples of community centres, home visits and support for children and families. Children’s rights came up too, along with the need for real evidence when deciding what support someone should receive.

SUPPORT FOR PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES
The discussion also covered care, financial help and the organisations that support families with disabilities. Having a service available on paper is one thing; making sure people can actually access it is another.

THE MONEY SIDE OF A PROJECT
We talked about budgets, staffing and everyday running costs. A service needs more than a good idea if it is going to continue helping people. Different teams also need to communicate with one another.

WORKING IN SOCIAL SERVICES
We briefly heard about career paths in social services, including learning policies and doing practical service work before moving into other roles, such as design. There are a lot of people and jobs behind one community project.

pages.title: CO-CREATION TOOLS & CREATIVE THINKING.
pages.intro: Lots of ways to collect, sort and combine ideas when working in a group.

children.text:
A WHOLE WEEK, NOT JUST ONE MOMENT
The lesson started with an imagined week in 2027 for Ben and his caregiver, Esther. We looked at their daily routine, activities and the help they might need. Seeing a whole week gives us a better picture of someone’s life than looking at just one event.

A FEW WORDS TO GET PEOPLE TALKING
Some of the activities used starters like “I like…”, “I wish…”, “I wonder…” and “I feel…”. They are simple, but they can make it less awkward for someone to share an idea or feeling.

BRAIN DUMP
For Brain Dump, we put down ideas quickly without worrying about whether they were good or bad. The point was to get everything out first instead of spending too long trying to make one perfect idea.

JOURNEY MAPPING
A journey map shows an experience step by step. We can mark what someone does, where they get stuck and what help they might need. It helps us see the part of a journey that is easy to miss when we only look at the starting point and destination.

ALTERNATE WORLDS
This one was quite different. The examples included a quiet beach, an amusement park, a hot-air balloon and time with loved ones. By imagining completely different places, we could find more ideas instead of always thinking in the same way.

ROSE, BUD AND THORN
Rose is something that works well. Thorn is a problem, and Bud is an idea with potential. It is a quick way to sort feedback without mixing all the comments together.

FEEDBACK MATRIX
We also had a matrix for things people liked, things they didn’t like, questions and new suggestions. Having separate spaces helps the group see what to keep and what to work on.

HOW MIGHT WE…?
This turns a problem into an open question, such as “How might we… for… so that…?”. We don’t have to jump straight to one answer, which gives the group room to explore different directions.

CREATIVE MATRIX AND POEMS
Finally, we looked at how to combine ideas using the Creative Matrix. POEMS stands for People, Objects, Environments, Messages and Services. Putting these together on a grid can help us see connections that are hard to notice on a blank page.

pages.title: COMMUNITY CARE & VOLUNTEERING.
pages.intro: A guest lecturer shared what it takes to support people and keep a community project going.

children.text:
COMMUNITY CARE AND VOLUNTEERING
This week, a guest lecturer came to talk about community care and volunteering. We heard about the support that older people, people with disabilities and their families may need. Some people feel very isolated, and there are not always enough trained social workers or other professionals around to help.

SMALL ACTIVITIES, REAL CONNECTIONS
The lecturer shared examples of universities and community groups working together. They organise activities like art and music, and also help caregivers share information and support each other. These might look like small things, but having somewhere to meet people can make a difference. The activities also have to suit the people taking part.

BEING A VOLUNTEER ISN’T ALWAYS EASY
Another part of the talk was about what happens behind the scenes. Volunteers can get tired, lose motivation or feel that their effort is not really helping. Communication between volunteers, caregivers and the people receiving support is not always smooth either. On top of that, some projects have limited money, no fixed place for activities and cannot reach everyone who needs them.

WHAT COULD WORK BETTER?
We also heard a few ideas for improving these services. Digital tools could make it easier to match people with support and keep records. Clear visual information might help people understand what services are available. Schools, hospitals and community organisations could work more closely together, and volunteers need proper training before starting. The talk covered a lot more than just showing up and helping for a few hours.

pages.title: REFRAMING IDEAS & WORKING THROUGH CONFLICT.
pages.intro: Stakeholder maps, choosing ideas and a different way to look at disagreements.

sections.name: 01 / WEEK 12 CLASS NOTES — Reframing and Conflict

children.text:
WHO IS INVOLVED IN A SERVICE?
We started with stakeholder maps. The circles showed different people connected to a project, including clients and families, staff and board members, partners and volunteers. Some are closely involved, while others support the project from further away. It is a useful way to check that we haven’t only thought about the main user.

ABSTRACT LADDERING / LOOK AT THE PROBLEM AGAIN
This week we also looked at Abstract Laddering. Instead of staying with the first problem we write down, we can ask bigger questions about why it matters, or look closer at how something happens. It helps a group find a clearer direction before jumping into solutions.

FROM A TAXI TO ‘TAXI-ING’
Another idea was reframing with ‘verb-ing’. The slides used a taxi as an example. Rather than only thinking about the taxi itself, we could look at the whole experience: finding one, getting in, talking to the driver, paying and getting out. There was also an example of using a simple video prototype to show this experience before making a final design.

BRAIN DUMP, DOT VOTING AND PRIORITIES
One class exercise asked us to list all the things we do as students each day, then the things we love doing. From there, the question became: How might we find more time for what matters most to us? We looked at dot voting, where each person gets four votes, and then a Prioritisation Matrix. The matrix compares how important something is with how difficult it might be. It gives a group a way to choose where to start when there are too many ideas.

CONFLICT DOESN’T HAVE TO BE THE END
The second part of the slides moved to conflict. People don’t always agree, and compromise doesn’t automatically mean everyone is happy. We talked about looking at conflict as something we can work through, instead of just deciding who is right or wrong.

THREE STEPS TO UNPACK A CONFLICT
First, try to understand what the disagreement is really about. The diagrams showed that a problem at work might also connect to family, friends, or even bigger systems and rules. Second, notice when we are getting stuck in blaming other people. Phrases like ‘I told you so’ or ‘Who did this?’ don’t always help us understand what happened. The last step was learning to speak more responsibly and listen properly.

VOCAB / SPEAKING AND LISTENING
We were introduced to VOCAB: Vulnerability, Ownership, Communication, Acceptance and Boundaries. The activity asked one person to share a conflict they felt stuck in, while the others listened with curiosity rather than rushing to judge or give advice. It was a different way to think about communication, especially when a group has different opinions.

pages.title: INCLUSION STARTS WITH “I”.
pages.intro: Self-care, vulnerability and thinking about the kind of designer I want to become.

sections.name: 01 / WEEK 13 CLASS NOTES — Inclusion, Self-Care & Ethos

children.text:
INCLUSION STARTS WITH “I”
The first slide said that inclusion starts with “I”. We looked at three words: Innovation, Integrity and Inter-dependence. I liked how the slides put them together. Trying new ideas is important, but it should never mean forgetting the rights and dignity of the people we are designing or working for.

LOOKING AFTER YOURSELF FIRST
Another part of the class was about starting with ourselves. One example used the oxygen mask on a plane: you need to put your own mask on before helping someone else. We also saw the words “I am enough”. It was a reminder that caring for others shouldn’t mean completely forgetting about yourself.

WHAT GIVES YOU ENERGY?
The slides asked two simple questions: What nourishes you, and what depletes you? There was also a monthly wellness check with things like mood, sleep, energy, time for yourself and relationships. I think these are the kinds of questions we don’t always stop to ask when we are busy working on projects.

VULNERABILITY AND THE LITTLE THINGS
We saw messages about trusting yourself, being open to vulnerability and not underestimating small details. One slide described vulnerability as a gift because it can help people connect. Another said that little things can make big things happen. These ideas were less about making a perfect design and more about how we treat ourselves and other people.

WHAT IS MY HCD ETHOS?
The last part turned to our own values as Human-Centred Designers. The slides reminded us not to compromise our ethos. There was also an interesting comparison: a human-centred designer is like a microphone, helping people whose voices are often missed to be heard. This connects with the reason I enjoy listening to other people’s stories. I want design to start with real people, not just my own ideas.

A LETTER TO 2030
We were also shown an activity about writing a letter to our future selves in 2030, along with the Paradoxical Commandments. The final message was that big journeys begin with small steps. It feels like a good way to end a course that has been about learning from people and slowly working out what kind of designer I want to be.
